# BiHeat

*two matrices in one heatmap*

<!-- badges: start -->
[![R-CMD-check](https://github.com/gcol33/BiHeat/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/gcol33/BiHeat/actions/workflows/R-CMD-check.yaml)
[![Codecov test coverage](https://codecov.io/gh/gcol33/BiHeat/graph/badge.svg)](https://app.codecov.io/gh/gcol33/BiHeat)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-yellow.svg)](https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT)
<!-- badges: end -->

BiHeat draws two numeric matrices of the same shape in one heatmap, such as observed and predicted values, a mean and its variance, or correlations and their p-values.

Each cell is split along a diagonal. The upper triangle shows the value from one matrix and the lower triangle the value from the other, each on its own colour gradient, and the plots are built with [ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org). Both values for a row and column sit in the same cell, so you can see where the two matrices agree and where they differ, and decide which cells to look at more closely.

BiHeat supports:

- **Separate or shared colour scales.** Each triangle gets its own range when the matrices measure different things, or both share one range when their values are directly comparable.
- **Matrices with different row or column names.** [`breed()`](https://gillescolling.com/BiHeat/reference/breed.html) aligns the two on their shared names and reports the Pearson and Spearman correlation, RMSE, MAE and the number of missing cells.
- **Split cells inside a ggplot.** [`geom_biheat()`](https://gillescolling.com/BiHeat/reference/geom_biheat.html) draws the same cells as a layer, so facets, coordinate systems and other layers work as usual, and the `fill` scale stays free for them.
- **Legends for figure assembly.** `bi_legend()` returns the paired colour key as a standalone grob, for figures where the panel is assembled separately.

Other packages draw related displays. [corrplot](https://cran.r-project.org/package=corrplot) has `corrplot.mixed()`, which draws one display above the diagonal of a correlation matrix and another below it. [ComplexHeatmap](https://bioconductor.org/packages/ComplexHeatmap/) can split a cell through a custom `cell_fun`, alongside its clustering and annotation tools. BiHeat splits every cell of two plain matrices and gives each half its own gradient.

## Installation

```r
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("gcol33/BiHeat")
```

## Usage

1. Draw the heatmap from two matrices with `biheat()`.
2. For more control, pair the matrices with `breed()`, set rendering options with `incubate()` and draw with `plot()`.
3. Pull the cell values back out as a data frame with `comes_out()`.

```{r quick, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Heatmap of 6 species by 8 sites in which every cell is split along its diagonal; the upper triangle shows the observed value on a white-to-red gradient and the lower triangle the predicted value on a white-to-blue gradient, and the two triangles of each cell have similar shades because the predictions differ from the observations by small noise"}
library(BiHeat)

set.seed(1)
species   <- LETTERS[1:6]
sites     <- letters[1:8]
observed  <- matrix(runif(48), 6, 8, dimnames = list(species, sites))
noise     <- matrix(rnorm(48, sd = 0.1), 6, 8)
predicted <- observed + noise

biheat(observed, predicted)
```

The first matrix fills the upper triangle (white to red) and the second the lower triangle (white to blue). Where the two disagree, the halves of a cell differ in shade.

The input is two numeric matrices. Where both carry row or column names, they are matched on the names they share; an axis without names on both sides is matched by position and needs the same length. [Getting started with BiHeat](https://gillescolling.com/BiHeat/articles/biheat.html) describes how the matrices are aligned and how missing cells are drawn.

## Pairing, styling and drawing in steps

`biheat()` is a shortcut for three steps. `breed()` pairs the two matrices into a clutch, an object holding both matrices aligned on their shared names together with their comparison statistics:

```{r clutch}
clutch <- breed(observed, predicted)
clutch
```

`incubate()` adds rendering options to a clutch, and each call adds to the options set before. `plot()` draws it:

```r
clutch |>
  incubate(scale = "shared", split = "up") |>
  plot()
```

The verbs take a clutch and return one, so they chain. `switch_sides()` swaps which matrix is on top, `straighten()` flips the direction of the diagonal and `bothways()` toggles between separate and shared colour scales:

```r
clutch |>
  switch_sides() |>
  straighten() |>
  bothways() |>
  plot()
```

## Separate or shared colour scales

- `scale = "separate"` (the default) gives the upper and lower triangles their own ranges. Use it when the two matrices measure different things, such as a correlation and its p-value or a mean and its variance.
- `scale = "shared"` puts both triangles on one range, so the colours of the two halves can be compared directly. Use it when the matrices are in the same units, such as observed and predicted values or the accuracy of two models.

[Styling and layout](https://gillescolling.com/BiHeat/articles/styling.html) covers palettes, printed values, cell geometry, skewed values and the order of rows and columns.

## Split cells inside a ggplot

`geom_biheat()` draws the split cells as a ggplot2 layer from a data frame with one row per cell, which is the shape `comes_out()` returns:

```r
library(ggplot2)

cells <- comes_out(clutch)

ggplot(cells, aes(col, row, upper = upper, lower = lower)) +
  geom_biheat() +
  theme_biheat()
```

Each triangle carries its own gradient, so neither uses the `fill` scale, which stays free for another layer. [Split cells inside a ggplot](https://gillescolling.com/BiHeat/articles/geom-biheat.html) shows faceting, continuous axes and layers drawn on top.

## Documentation

Start with [Getting started with BiHeat](https://gillescolling.com/BiHeat/articles/biheat.html): from two matrices to a split heatmap, how the matrices are aligned and what `plot()` returns.

- [Styling and layout](https://gillescolling.com/BiHeat/articles/styling.html): palettes, printed values, cell geometry and row and column order.
- [Split cells inside a ggplot](https://gillescolling.com/BiHeat/articles/geom-biheat.html): the `geom_biheat()` layer with facets, continuous axes and other layers.
- [Full reference](https://gillescolling.com/BiHeat/reference/): every function, grouped by job.

## Citation

```{r citation, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cit <- citation("BiHeat")
fence <- function(lang, x) cat("```", lang, "\n", paste(x, collapse = "\n\n"), "\n```\n\n", sep = "")
cat(attr(cit, "mheader"), "\n\n", sep = "")
fence("text", format(cit, style = "text"))
cat("BibTeX:\n\n")
fence("bibtex", format(cit, style = "bibtex"))
```

Download the citation as [BibTeX](https://gillescolling.com/BiHeat/BiHeat.bib) or [RIS](https://gillescolling.com/BiHeat/BiHeat.ris).
